title: Characterizing Reaction Types through Linear Free-Energy Relationships in Cavities
authors: Jillian G. Hoffstadt, Davis M. Welakuh, Norah M. Hoffmann
abstract: Polaritonic chemistry holds the promise of controlling chemical reactivity through confined light-matter interactions, yet how reactions respond inside optical cavities remains debated. Here, we take a more zoomed-out view, inspired by electrostatic catalysis. We extend nonempirical linear free-energy relationships to cavity-modified reactions and show that their behavior falls into four distinct reaction types set by simple response-crossing rules. Reactions can follow conventional Bell-Evans-Polanyi (BEP) or counterintuitive Opposite-BEP behavior regardless of cavity tuning, or switch between the two as the cavity frequency is varied. We establish this picture analytically and demonstrate it in the Shin Metiu model and in four molecular reactions treated with ab initio electronic-structure methods. Even at this deliberately coarse-grained level, cavity-modified reactivity already shows qualitatively different and strongly counterintuitive behavior, including reactions that switch character with cavity frequency. Yet this complexity can still be reduced to a simple competition between permanent-dipole and polarizability responses. This reaction-type classification therefore provides a new route to organize and anticipate cavity-modified reactivity.
summary: This paper develops a classification scheme for chemical reactions occurring within optical cavities by extending linear free-energy relationships. By analyzing the cavity-modified reaction prefactor, the authors categorize reactions into four types based on how their behavior (BEP or Opposite-BEP) changes as the cavity frequency is tuned. This provides a predictive tool for understanding cavity-controlled chemical reactivity.
main_problem: The paper addresses how chemical reaction rates are modified and characterized when occurring inside optical cavities, moving beyond general debates in polaritonic chemistry.
main_result: Reactions are classified into four distinct types based on how the cavity-modified linear free-energy relationship prefactor behaves as the cavity frequency is tuned. This classification predicts whether the reaction follows conventional (BEP) or counterintuitive (Opposite-BEP) behavior, or switches between them.
method: The authors extend nonempirical Linear Free-Energy Relationships (LFERs) by deriving an analytical expression for the reaction prefactor, which depends on the permanent-dipole and polarizability responses of the molecules.
model_or_system: The system involves molecular reactions (tested on Shin Metiu model and four ab-initio examples) coupled to an optical cavity. The analysis focuses on the frequency dependence of the coupling via the polarizability $\alpha(\omega)$.
key_observables: The LFER prefactor ($m$), which determines the reaction type (BEP vs. Opposite-BEP), and the dependence of $m$ on the cavity frequency ($\omega$).
important_parameters: Cavity frequency ($\omega$), permanent-dipole moments ($\mu$), and frequency-dependent polarizabilities ($\alpha(\omega)$).
main_assumptions: The analysis is coarse-grained, approximating free energy changes by neglecting entropic and thermal contributions, and assuming the coupling is weak enough that the reaction pathway is not fundamentally altered by the cavity.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the four reaction types (I-IV) based on the sign and crossing behavior of the prefactor $m$ versus $\omega$, and show the dipole and polarizability contributions leading to $m$ for specific molecular examples.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the theoretical framework by extending LFERs to cavities. It then analytically derives the prefactor $m$ based on molecular responses. The core of the work is the classification into four types based on response-crossing rules, which is demonstrated using both a simplified model (Shin Metiu) and rigorous ab-initio calculations on representative chemical reactions.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful, general framework for predicting chemical reactivity in structured light environments, linking macroscopic concepts like reaction type to fundamental molecular electronic properties (dipole/polarizability) and cavity tuning.
